subject: Bell's 1.2 GW AI bet runs on its own gas plants
bodyMarkdown:
The Globe and Mail reported Monday that Bell wants to quadruple its Saskatchewan AI project to 1.2 gigawatts, and that most of the new electricity would come from gas plants Bell builds itself, outside the provincial grid. The largest private capital investment in Saskatchewan's history turns out to be a plan to burn natural gas so two American companies can rent Canadian compute.

## What Bell actually announced

The venue was the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Premier Scott Moe and BCE chief executive Mirko Bibic on stage. Bell already has 300 megawatts under construction in the Rural Municipality of Sherwood outside Regina, with the first data halls due in service in the first half of 2027 and CoreWeave and Cerebras signed as anchor tenants. Monday's news adds up to 900 megawatts more in phases, and Bell puts the full buildout above $50 billion once you count its buildings, the tenants' servers and the power generation. CBC reported the province calling it the largest private capital investment in Saskatchewan history. The jobs figure is 500 permanent positions plus roughly 3,000 in security, logistics and maintenance. What I would underline is that this is a non-binding memorandum of understanding with the province rather than a signed contract.

## Where the electricity comes from

Saskatchewan's data centre framework runs on **Bring Your Own Power**, a rule that a new project must supply its own electricity instead of drawing on SaskPower, so it cannot squeeze the grid or eat into the power the province sells elsewhere. The Logic reported that the bulk of Bell's expansion depends on new natural gas generation built off the provincial system, which would leave Bell's AI business majority gas-fired if all of it goes ahead. For scale, 1,200 megawatts is close to a quarter of everything Saskatchewan can generate today, a fleet the Canada Energy Regulator puts a little above 5,300 megawatts. Bell says the sites use closed-loop cooling and need no municipal water. Locally that has settled nothing. CBC reported NDP technology critic Brittney Senger saying the plan arrived with "absolutely zero public consultation", and CJME reported Tuesday that the NDP now wants a moratorium on data centre construction.

## Whether $50 billion is really Bell's

Mostly it is not, and I think that is the honest way to read the headline. Bell's own money buys land, shells and connections, while the tenants buy the chips. BCE's guidance this year has capital spending up $1.3 billion, mostly for Saskatchewan, with adjusted earnings per share and free cash flow expected to fall, the dividend held at $1.75 after last year's cut, and about $400 million of one-time setup fees and customer prepayments this year. The company says it will not issue common shares to fund it. So the business is landlord economics, long leases on space and power sold to CoreWeave and Cerebras, whose own customers have to keep paying through the 2030s. Carney is chasing $1 trillion of investment over five years, and BNN Bloomberg reported the summit drew investors from nearly 30 countries.

## The takeaway

Before treating 1.2 gigawatts as real, watch whether that memorandum turns into a binding agreement, and watch how the gas plants move through permitting, since money.ca reported the first 300 megawatts went ahead without an environmental review. If you own BCE for the dividend, the number to check is free cash flow in the third quarter results this fall, not the $50 billion in the headline. And if the AI trade cools before 2030, Saskatchewan is left holding gas plants built for tenants who no longer need them, which is the risk nobody on that stage wanted to price.
